items.title: Eliyan’s $1 Billion Valuation Signals AI Networking Is the Next Battleground | Investing.com
items.snippet: The Santa Clara-based startup announced Wednesday that it raised $145 million in...
items.raw_snippet:
The Santa Clara-based startup announced Wednesday that it raised $145 million in a Series C funding round, giving the company a $1 billion valuation. The oversubscribed round was led by Seligman Ventures, with new strategic investments from Cisco Investments and Lumentum, alongside existing investors. As part of the deal, Seligman Ventures Managing Partner Umesh Padval will join Eliyan’s board.

## AI Chips Are Getting Faster. Data Movement Isn’t. [...] ## Cisco and Lumentum’s Investment Matters More Than the Funding

The financing itself is significant, but the names behind it may be even more important.

Cisco has spent decades building networking equipment, while Lumentum is a major supplier of optical networking technology. Neither company is making a simple venture capital investment.

Their backing suggests they believe networking is becoming one of the most valuable layers of the AI infrastructure stack. [...] That shift has already played out once before.

In 2019, Nvidia acquired Mellanox for $6.9 billion, giving it control over one of the industry’s leading networking businesses. That acquisition is now widely viewed as one of Nvidia’s smartest strategic moves because AI performance increasingly depends on how efficiently chips communicate with one another.

Cisco and Lumentum appear to be making a similar bet, but through an independent company rather than building the technology themselves.

items.raw_snippet:
More on AI: Sam Altman Says Even the Power of AI Will Never Lead to a Shorter Work Week [...] Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech

The business world has quickly learned that there’s such a thing as using too much AI, as they get slammed with outrageous token bills.

Now, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is warning of another way that embracing AI could doom a business.

In an interview Sunday, Nadella cautioned against sharing too much information, ranging from proprietary data to the prompts entered, with a third-party AI model. [...] That’s a striking claim — and an ironic one, since outsourcing your thinking is arguably exactly the point of using AI, of which Microsoft is a leading vendor. Nadella, in a nutshell, is saying that heavily relying on proprietary AI software could also be a company’s undoing.
